source.title: Beyond Suffixes: Token Position in GCG Adversarial Attacks on Large Language Models
source.authors: Hicham Eddoubi; U. Abdullahi; Fadi Hassan

page_placements.theme: Optimized input attacks have conditional transfer and placement effects

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether adversarial suffix attacks bypass safety and whether changing token placement affects harmful-completion rates, using GCG rather than the original studies’ methods.
record.gate_note: The paper reports harmful-prompt ASR for GCG attacks optimized and evaluated at different token positions. It also reports attention-allocation findings, but these are not per-response-position KL measurements. Table 2's detailed cross-model cells are flattened in the supplied text and are not reliably assignable to every attack–target pair; the paper's explicit aggregate statement about transferability is recorded instead.
record.test_reason: It reports harmful-compliance ASR (GPT-4 judge) for GCG adversarial prompt tokens against five chat models. That bears on V4's claim that adversarial suffixes defeat refusal. The method differs from the originals' prefilling, but the question is the same: do input manipulations bypass refusal? Its main question, token placement within the prompt, is not itself a V4 claim.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that adversarial-token position, in both optimization and evaluation, substantially changes GCG ASR in white-box and cross-model settings. They argue that fixed-suffix evaluation overestimates robustness and that attention as a saliency metric is 'myopic' and position-dependent.
record.recipe_differences: Uses GCG optimization of adversarial prompt tokens and evaluates prefix/suffix placement; it does not fine-tune models, prefill compliant response tokens, or measure aligned-versus-base per-token KL.
record.method_sensitivity: Attack success varies with adversarial-token placement, optimization position, source model, and target model.

fits_no_version.finding: ASR depends on where adversarial tokens sit in the prompt and where they were optimized. Allowing either placement raises ASR, by up to 49 points in cross-model transfer.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Jailbreak success of optimized adversarial tokens depends on their placement in the prompt; fixed-suffix evaluation underestimates risk.

fits_no_version.finding: Attention on adversarial vs goal tokens differs by placement and layer. Successful prefix attacks get little late-layer attention.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Attention-based saliency of jailbreak tokens is position- and layer-dependent.

record.peer_reviewed: I Can’t Believe It’s Not Better Workshop @ ICLR 2026; arXiv preprint
record.problems: The study samples 100 harmful prompts, uses GPT-4 as a single judge, and reports no uncertainty estimates. Attention results are presented in figures without numeric values. The supplied Table 2 layout is flattened, limiting reliable extraction of individual cross-model cells.
record.rows_left_out: Detailed individual Table 2 cross-model cells are not separately recorded because the supplied flattened layout does not reliably preserve all attack-model and target-model assignments. The explicit aggregate transfer result is recorded as X1.

untested.parts: Prefilling a compliant response opening and decoding changes. Only GCG prompt-token attacks are tested, with greedy decoding.
Per-position KL between aligned and base models; not measured. Attention analysis is over input tokens, not response positions.

missing.what: Cross-model transfer ASR@k=2 per attack–target pair, with increments. The cells are readable: e.g. Llama-2 target 0–1% except self (36/41%); Qwen target 0–5% except self; Vicuna target 52–99%; Mistral target 31–94%.
No-attack baseline ASR for each model. It is not reported in the paper, so the rows cannot be compared with a control.

record.verdict_notes: The paper does not frame itself around shallow alignment; its V4 relevance is only that GCG prompt tokens bypass refusal. Placing tokens as a prompt prefix is not response prefilling. Success requires a GPT-4 harm score of 5, a strict threshold. The setup is 100 AdvBench prompts, a single seed, 250 GCG iterations, and no uncertainty estimates. Vicuna and Mistral have weak safety tuning, which inflates support; the well-aligned Llama-2 resists more.

versions.untested_parts: Harmful fine-tuning and safety loss after fine-tuning.
Benign fine-tuning and its effect on harmful compliance.
Per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models across response positions.
The paper tests GCG adversarial-token placement, including suffix attacks and prefix/suffix relocation. It does not test compliant response-opening prefills or decoding changes.
Whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behaviour.
Whether training data or objective causes safety to be shallow.
Training to deepen safety and whether that training holds up.
